summary: Unit 1 design: base on arena candidate 1 (opus), trimmed; the sonnet judge picked the same base
why: It keeps an Entry from ever holding a stale hash, makes next_entry the only way to mint an entry, and links lines on stored seq and hash so problems don't cascade. Its id-format, length-cap and line-size rules were dropped as unrequired by S2 or S3

evidence: golden head 2465b40d…25da reproduced by an independent Node verifier
summary: Canonical form is RFC 8785 (JCS) restricted to integers within ±(2^53−1) and keys matching [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}, raw UTF-8
why: An auditor can check hashes with an off-the-shelf JCS library; with no floats and ASCII keys, JCS has no ambiguous cases. Pure-ASCII output (the sonnet candidate) was rejected because no standard defines it

summary: A line's bytes must equal the canonical encoding of what it parses to; verify never normalizes before hashing
why: Without this, a whitespace or escape edit re-canonicalizes to the same hash and "any changed byte is detected" would be false

summary: Unit 1 ships ledger verify RUN_FOLDER with exit codes 0 verified, 1 failed, 2 usage or read error, and lists every problem as path:line: kind: message
why: The task scopes verify to one run folder; the no-argument and --base forms belong to unit 4. A missing ledger in a run folder counts as failed, not as an I/O error

summary: Chain-only verify does not detect entries cut from the end or a suffix rewritten with recomputed hashes; this is stated in the spec, the CLI output and a test
why: The hash has no secret, so a prefix of a valid chain is valid. Seals and verify --base (unit 4) anchor the head in git

summary: Format v1 has no floats, so S3's spend example {usd, ...} can't hold dollars as written; proposed usd_micros, left open for Beau
why: Float canonicalization differs across languages and would break cross-language verification. Per AGENTS.md the spec conflict is raised, not silently resolved

evidence: Commit "fix(ledger): harden verify against hostile ledgers"
S3 "Format v1" now sets a 32-level nesting limit
summary: Interrogate (correctness, security, maintainer) on opus and sonnet found a nesting-depth crash, terminal escapes in messages, and mutable Entry data; all fixed
why: The charter requires interrogate on every PR. Both models independently found the depth crash, the mutable data and verify .; each fix has a regression test and a mutant that the suite catches

alternatives: pessimistic lock around build and write

summary: The repo sink's write is a compare-and-append under flock on ledger.jsonl; append re-chains on a lost race
why: The sink, not each caller, guarantees one chain, so a library caller such as agent-queue can't fork it. Locking the ledger itself leaves no lock file to commit

summary: ledger init writes seq 1 as a state entry with data {state: started}, created through a temp file and os.link
why: Verify rejects an empty ledger, so a run needs a real first entry; os.link fails if the ledger exists, so two inits can't both win and no reader sees a half-written file

summary: Every write takes --actor as S2 JSON and append takes --run; neither has a default
why: The stdlib can't read policy.yaml, and an inherited default would let a subagent write under its parent's id, which S2 forbids. S3's command table named neither flag; the CLI is not frozen until the public-api gate

summary: Imported entries keep their original actor, type and text; ts is the chaining time and data.imported holds source, source_ts and by
why: A ts earlier than the write would let any entry be backdated unseen. The approval keeps Beau as actor because v1 requires a human on approvals; data.imported.by says an agent typed it in. Beau's actor gained on_behalf_of lyddonb@github, which S2 requires

summary: The lock uses fcntl, so append, init and show need Linux or macOS; verify still runs anywhere
why: The charter's CI is Ubuntu and every known machine is macOS; a Windows lock (msvcrt) would be untested code. fcntl is imported lazily so a missing one is a clear error, not a crash

summary: Correction to seq 13 and 14: imported_seqs [2,9] means seq 2 to 9 inclusive; init does not need fcntl, only append and show do
why: Interrogate found both. The ledger is append-only, so a correcting entry replaces an edit

summary: Unit 3 (redaction and session add) started on feat/ledger-unit3-redaction
why: Units 1 and 2 and the spend follow-up are merged (PRs 1 to 3); Beau said to start unit 3

summary: Redaction fails closed: spans from all patterns merged on the original text, then confirmed by an idempotent second pass and a scan of decoded JSON strings
why: A miss commits a secret to git history (charter Security notes), so unconfirmed text must be refused, never guessed at

summary: A JSON line whose decoded strings still match is rebuilt from its redacted value instead of refusing the whole transcript
why: Tool results hold JSON nested in strings, where the text scan can't see a quoted key; refusing every such transcript would keep most real sessions out of the archive

summary: Policy redact_patterns are read with a strict reader that takes [] or single-quoted block items only, and errors on anything else
why: The standard library has no YAML parser and a dependency is a gate; silently skipping a policy pattern would be a miss, so an unreadable policy stops the write

summary: Git LFS routing over lfs_over_mb is deferred to unit 7; an archive over 20 MB compressed prints a warning
why: lfs_over_mb lives in policy audit.sessions, which unit 7 reads; one real transcript (91 MB raw) compressed to 24 MB, so the warning fires in practice

summary: 26 real Claude Code transcripts (52 KB to 91 MB) archived with session add: 0 refused, chain verified, an independent grep found no leftover keys
why: Tests prove the planted corpus; this proves real transcripts archive without false refusals and at usable speed (about 0.5 s per MB)

summary: Four deliberate breaks of the redactor (no JSON rebuild, no confirm, no span merge, no escaped-quote handling) each fail the suite
why: Shows the planted-secret tests catch the failure modes they claim to, not only that they pass

data.independent: same model family; no cross-family review for unit 3, per the charter

summary: Two-model security review of unit 3 (opus, sonnet): 5 blockers, 9 warnings, all fixed or answered in ffbd501 and 01c58c9
why: The charter gives redaction the security lens. Opus found secrets surviving double escaping and in data keys; sonnet found sk- matching inside words, which corrupted session ids, and refusals that could never be retried

summary: Confirmation now covers every decoded view of a line; a JSON line that still matches or no longer parses is rebuilt from its original value
why: Opus showed five secrets surviving two layers of escaping; a real transcript showed the old key pattern could break a JSON escape, so redaction must never corrupt a line it then calls confirmed

summary: Left open: session ids that differ only in case collide on macOS
why: Claude Code session ids are lowercase UUIDs, so this needs a hand-picked --session to happen; worth a check when unit 4 touches INDEX.jsonl

summary: After the fixes: 28 real transcripts (148 MB) redacted with 0 refusals and 0 JSON lines broken; 137 tests pass on 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; the opus probe script now finds no leak
why: Shows the hardened confirmation doesn't refuse real sessions, and that the reviewers' own repros are fixed, not only the tests written for them

summary: Unit 4 (seal, INDEX.jsonl, verify --base) started on feat/ledger-unit4-seal
why: Unit 3 merged as PR 4; Beau said to start unit 4

summary: A seal's prev is the final hash and data.commit names HEAD; seal refuses unless the ledger at HEAD is the file on disk, so the commit holds the sealed head
why: Storing the final hash again would be redundant and could disagree; requiring the committed head lets verify read the ledger at that commit and compare

summary: Seals need merge commits; squash and rebase merges drop the sealed commit and verify reports seal-commit. Added HUMAN_TASKS H6
why: The repo allows all three merge styles; anchoring a branch commit only works if it reaches main, and choosing merge settings is Beau's call

summary: verify --base compares the base commit's blobs with HEAD's (ls-tree with modes, cat-file), never the working tree
why: Opus proved two-PR attacks that rewrote merged history through a symlinked .audit and a .gitattributes encoding, both because the PR side was read from disk

summary: Three-model review of unit 4 (opus, sonnet, Cursor grok-4.7-xhigh-fast): 2 blockers and 9 warnings, all fixed or documented
why: The charter staffs a cross-family review for unit 4. Opus found the --base bypasses; sonnet found a seal race and a half-done seal; grok found seals read by a different git path than the base check

summary: 173 tests pass on 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; 11 deliberate breaks each fail them; opus's attack scripts now fail at PR 1; verify --base passes against every past merge of this repo
why: Shows the guards are tested, the reviewers' proven attacks are closed, and the real history is append-only

summary: Unit 5 (charter new, check, approve) started on feat/ledger-unit5-charter
why: Unit 4 merged as PR 5; Beau said to start unit 5

summary: Charter front matter is read by a strict reader for a YAML subset that refuses anything it can't read exactly, and must agree with PyYAML wherever it accepts a value
why: A dependency is a gate and the M0 charter is approved byte for byte; a field read differently from what the human saw could approve the wrong budget

summary: Approval state is derived from the ledger: approved when the latest human approval names the file's sha256, stale after an edit
why: S1 says edits return a charter to draft; deriving it from the hash needs no extra state and can't drift

summary: approve requires the sha256 prefix the human read from check, and a relayed approval must quote it
why: Opus showed the relaying agent could edit between the human's read and the approve call; binding the quote to the hash makes the archived transcript prove which version was approved, until signing in M4

summary: Two-model review of unit 5 (opus, sonnet): 5 blockers and 15 warnings or nits, all fixed
why: Opus found a hidden U+2028 that showed the human one budget and the reader another, and approval not bound to reviewed bytes; sonnet found placeholder keys passing, crashes on bad input and loose value types

summary: 207 tests pass on 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; 18 deliberate breaks each fail them; the reader agrees with PyYAML on 40,000 generated values; the real M0 charter checks complete and approved at seq 24
why: Shows the checks are tested, the reader can't be read differently by a real YAML parser, and the existing approved charter still validates

summary: The required ledger-verify job runs from pull_request_target: the base branch's Action checks the PR's merge commit as data and never runs its code
why: Opus showed a pull_request workflow, and the Action under uses: ./, come from the PR itself, so a PR could edit the check that judges it

summary: A pull request's base is its merge commit's first parent; merge queues use their base; other events without a base fail
why: origin/<base> can be newer than the merge ref and fail an honest PR; a merge queue had no base and only warned

summary: ledger scan adds the base's redact patterns to the change's, accepts only real placeholder names, and bounds size and time
why: Opus proved a PR could drop a policy pattern and leak its secret in the same change, and that a token could hide in a fake placeholder; both reviewers measured unbounded scan cost

summary: Two-model review of unit 6 (opus, sonnet): 2 blockers and 7 warnings, all fixed
